opus-5.5.text:
I think that impression is half right, and the half that's wrong matters a lot.

The part that's right is that the cost of producing code has collapsed. A lot of the work that used to take a junior engineer a week, like writing a CRUD backend, wiring up a frontend, or adding a CLI flag and its tests, an agent can now do in minutes. For people who aren't professional programmers, that's genuinely liberating. They can build small tools for themselves that never would have existed before.

But "writing code" was never the hard part of most serious software. In my own work on inference systems like vLLM, the hard part is deciding *what* to build and understanding *why* something behaves the way it does. Why does throughput drop at a certain batch size? Why does a kernel that's fast on one GPU become slow on another? Why does a change that looks harmless break some user's deployment that we've never seen? Those questions are about the whole system: the hardware, the scheduler, the memory layout, and the real workloads people run. An agent can produce a plausible patch, but whether that patch is *correct* in all the situations that matter is a much harder question, and today it still needs someone with deep context to judge.

There's actually an interesting side effect for open-source maintainers. Contributions have become very cheap to generate, but review hasn't become cheap. We get many more PRs that look reasonable on the surface, and the bottleneck shifts entirely to review, testing, and design. So in some sense the scarce resource is no longer people who can write code. It's people who can tell good code from code that merely looks good, and who can hold the architecture in their head.

So my view is that coding agents have made *simple* software easy to write, and they've made complex software faster to iterate on. But they've also raised the bar on taste and understanding. The engineers who will do well are the ones who use agents to move faster while still deeply understanding the systems underneath. If you treat the agent as a replacement for understanding, you end up with a lot of code that nobody can actually maintain.

r001.rationale: The response says serious software requires understanding the whole system and that humans with deep context must judge whether an agent’s patch is correct.

r002.rationale: It says software cannot be maintained when the agent is treated as a replacement for human understanding, and identifies maintainers’ review and architectural understanding as scarce human work.

r003.rationale: It says agents can produce plausible patches, but human judgment, review, testing, and design remain necessary to determine whether the work is correct.

fable-5.1.text:
I think that impression is half right and half an illusion, and the half that's an illusion is the dangerous part.

What coding agents have genuinely made easy is the "last mile" of software: given a clear spec, a well-understood stack, and plenty of similar code in the training data, an agent can produce a working CRUD app, a script, a demo, a plugin, in minutes. That part used to take a junior engineer a week. Now it takes an afternoon. So if your definition of "software" is that layer, yes, it has become easy, and I don't think we should be nostalgic about it.

But most of the software that actually matters is not that layer. Take the kind of work I do on vLLM. The hard problems there are not "write a function." They are things like: how do you make CUDA graphs coexist with dynamic batching, how do you make torch.compile not recompile on every new shape, how does a change to the scheduler interact with memory fragmentation under real traffic. The difficulty is not in typing the code. It is in understanding the system well enough to know what code to type, and in knowing what will break three layers away when you change something. An agent can write you a hundred lines very fast, but whether those hundred lines are correct depends on knowledge that often does not exist in any public text, because the people who have it are the twenty or thirty engineers who have debugged that specific interaction.

So I would describe it this way: coding agents have compressed the distance between "I know what I want" and "it exists." They have not compressed the distance between "I have a vague idea" and "I know what I want." And in infrastructure, in performance work, in anything where correctness is defined by physics or hardware rather than by a product manager, that second distance is almost all of the work.

There is also a trap for the ecosystem. When writing code is cheap, people write a lot more code, and a lot of it is mediocre. We see this in open source already: pull requests that are obviously agent-generated, that compile and pass the happy-path tests, and that quietly misunderstand the design. Reviewing those is now the bottleneck. In some sense the agent has moved the cost from the author to the maintainer, and maintainers are a much scarcer resource than authors.

What I tell students is: the agent is an excellent amplifier of taste. If you understand the system deeply, it lets you move at ten times your speed. If you don't, it lets you produce wrong things at ten times your speed, and it will do so confidently. The skill that is becoming more valuable, not less, is the ability to form a precise mental model of a system and to judge whether a piece of code is right. That is also, not coincidentally, the hardest thing to learn, and it is the thing you cannot shortcut by asking the agent to do it for you.

r001.rationale: The response says the hardest work is understanding the system and deciding what code to write, and that humans must judge whether the code is right.

r002.rationale: It identifies reviewing agent-generated pull requests as a bottleneck and says maintainers are scarce, explicitly describing ongoing human maintenance work.

r003.rationale: It says agents can generate software quickly, but correct results still depend on human system knowledge and judgment.

astra-6.text:
I think that impression mixes up two things: making code easier to generate and making software easier to build. Coding agents have clearly helped with the first. You can describe an idea and get something running much faster, and that’s valuable.

But getting something running is only part of the job. You still need to decide what it should do, understand how it fits into an existing system, and know whether the result is correct. Sometimes the difficult part is even figuring out what “correct” means.

So I wouldn’t say all software has become easy to write. The bottleneck is shifting. When producing code becomes cheaper, your ability to specify the problem and evaluate the solution becomes more important. A convincing demo can happen very quickly; dependable software still requires judgment.

r001.rationale: It says people still need to decide what software should do and understand how it fits into an existing system, conveying that system design requires human involvement.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss long-term software maintenance.

r003.rationale: It says human judgment remains important, but does not state that AI can complete most of the work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that impression confuses writing code with building software. Coding agents make it much easier to get a first version running, and that’s a real improvement. But you still have to decide what the software should do, whether the result is correct, and how it should behave when something goes wrong.

The difficulty also depends on the task. If you can describe the problem clearly and check the answer cheaply, an agent can be very effective. If the requirements are ambiguous or failures are hard to detect, generating more code doesn’t necessarily get you closer to a solution.

So I’d say agents have made many coding tasks easier. They haven’t made all software easy to build. A lot of the work moves toward specifying the problem and verifying the result.

r001.rationale: The response says people must decide what software should do and verify results, but it does not state that high-level system design still requires human involvement.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss long-term software maintenance.

r003.rationale: The response identifies decisions and verification that people still handle, but does not say this remains necessary even when AI can complete most of the development work.
